turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through, grab a seat. What's been playing on your mind with the diabetes?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh it's a bit of a saga, if I'm honest. I've been meaning to come for weeks, the sugars have been all over the shop, work's been flat out, and I keep telling myself I'll sort the little book out and then I just don't.

[SEG0003] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm on the sugar tablets, the metformin, plus the night pen, and I reckon I'm doing most of it right, but some mornings I look at that meter and think, that can't be right.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's unpack it slowly, no rush. When you say all over the shop, what are you actually seeing?

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting, it's one-eighty-something. Sometimes one-eighty-two, sometimes I swear it flashed one-ninety, and once it was one-seven-six, only I didn't write that down because the dog was going off and I was already late.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): And I don't even know if that machine speaks Australian numbers or the other ones. My brother-in-law posted it from the States years back and I've just kept buying the strips that fit.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then we can't treat one-eighty-something as gospel until we know the units. We'll park the meter for a bit. How have you been feeling in yourself, day to day?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Tired. Properly tired, not just a late one. I'm on the couch by half seven, and I'm thirsty all arvo, filling the bottle two, sometimes three times on shift.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Up to the loo once or twice a night as well. Not every single night, but most nights this last month or so. Drives my wife mad, the light in the hall.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any change in your weight with all that, or is it mainly the thirst and the tiredness?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I've dropped a bit, I think. Belt's on a tighter hole. I didn't get on the scales, so I won't make up a number for you.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine. The sugar tablets, the metformin — what are you actually swallowing, and when?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): One gram with breakfast and one gram with tea. The big white ones. Years I've been on those, and I don't miss them, they're the easy bit, they live next to the kettle.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good to hear. And the insulin, the night pen — walk me through what you dial.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Lantus, the clear one, grey cap. I dial eighteen units, round nine or half past, unless I've got an early start the next day.
[SEG0016] person_3 (NURSE): Sorry, can I jump in? Last month's chart is open here and it says insulin glargine twenty-four units at night. Same figure on the script from Dr Shah.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty-four? Nah, I've never dialled twenty-four. Some educator bloke started me at ten and said creep up, and I stopped at eighteen because I went woozy one morning. That was ages ago, mind you.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): So you say eighteen, and the file says twenty-four. I'm not going to guess which one is real. We'll leave the number blank until the pen's in front of us.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I can bring the pen, easy. It's in the fridge door, next to the margarine, which is a stupid spot, I know, but that's where it ended up.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): That'll help a lot. You mentioned early starts. What actually happens on those mornings?

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I skip it. If I'm on the six o'clock at the warehouse I don't take the Lantus the night before, because I got shaky once driving and I don't fancy that on the freeway. Mondays, Tuesdays, sometimes a Thursday.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin still goes in those days. It's only the pen I leave out. I know that's not what the leaflet says, but the leaflet doesn't do the M1 at five in the morning.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Roughly how many nights in a week do you reckon you inject?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, three or four? Could be more on a quiet week. I don't keep a tally, so don't pin me to four, I'll only get it wrong.
[SEG0025] person_3 (NURSE): When I asked out the front he said he takes it every night. That's what I put on the pre-screen, so this is different.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, yeah, I say that, because if I admit I skip it everyone has a go. I'm telling you the real version now. Sorry about the mix-up.

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd rather the real one, truly. So the doses are patchy, and the chart may not match the pen. I'm not going to call this uncontrolled diabetes, or a wrong script, not yet. It might be the missed doses, it might be that you're on less than we thought, it might be the meter counting in the wrong units, or something else like a urine infection or what you're eating, and I won't land on one today.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Eating's not flash, I'll give you that. Sausage roll from the servo most mornings, canteen's shut till eight, and a pie some arvos. Not every day. My wife packs a salad and I leave it in the fridge at home, regular as clockwork.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heard, and I'm not here to lecture you about pies. Any hypos lately, the shaky sweaty ones, apart from that drive?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. That freeway thing was maybe a year back. These days if I feel a bit off I have a barley sugar. Never needed the ambos, nothing dramatic.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the chest — pain, tightness, getting short of breath?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain, no tightness. I get puffed on the stairs at work, but that's me being unfit, not a chest thing. I can still talk while I'm doing it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the feet? Numbness, sores, anything you've clocked?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Toes on the right, and a bit on the left, tingly for months. Pins and needles when I first get up, it fades, then it's back around tea time. No sores. I do look, because Mum lost a toe and I'm not queuing up for that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): She had the type two as well, ended up on dialysis. That's the family ending I don't want. Dad was different, a heart attack at seventy-two, out of the blue.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry about your mum. We'll look at the feet properly in a minute. Eyes — any blurring, any floaters?

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Newspaper's fuzzy some mornings till I've blinked a few times. I had the photo thing, the retinal screen, at the optometrist in Parramatta, I want to say four months ago, and they posted a letter saying it was okay, no treatment. Letter's in the drawer with the rates notices.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): If that letter really says the retinas were fine four months ago, I don't need to send you again today. Bring it next time so I can read the actual line, not the memory of it.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I will. I had it in my hand this morning and then the kettle boiled and I walked out without it. Story of my life, that drawer.
[SEG0040] person_3 (NURSE): Obs before he came in: blood pressure one forty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight. He knocked back a finger-prick, said the home meter was enough.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks for that. One forty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight. So no clinic sugar on the slip.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I hate the lancet here, it's brutal. The one at home is finer, even if the numbers are dodgy.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shoes and socks off when you're ready and I'll have a look. Is there pain in the feet, or just that tingling?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the tingling. No pain, no redness. I stood on a nail at work back in March, didn't even break the skin, more of a fright than an injury.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both foot pulses are there, skin's intact, no ulcers, and no cracks between the toes. The monofilament is dull on the right big toe and the second toe, and it's normal on the left.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Dull, hey. I thought I felt something. Maybe I felt you pressing, not the little point. Figures, with the tingling.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's exactly why we use it. Any allergies I should have on the file — tablets, the insulin, anything else?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Penicillin was fine when I had it for a tooth. No rashes, no swelling, none of that.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Besides the metformin and the Lantus, anything else regular? Blood pressure, cholesterol?

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Perindopril, four milligrams, mornings, for the blood pressure, the diabetes clinic put me on it years back. That's the lot apart from a statin they tried, Crestor I think, which was stopped ages ago for muscle aches.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Crestor stopped for the muscle aches, and we won't restart it today. How long have you actually had the type two?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I was forty-six, I'm fifty-eight now, so twelve years, give or take. The exact month escapes me. Round my birthday, June-ish, but don't write June as if I'm sure.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Twelve years, and it's ongoing. Any operations along the way?

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Gallbladder out, keyhole, about six years back. Appendix is still in there, far as I know. And a vasectomy, ancient history, not relevant, I just don't know when to stop talking.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): All of it helps, you're alright. Smoking? Drink?

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked, not even as a kid. Beer on a Saturday, two or three, not through the week. I walk the dog, that's the exercise, twenty minutes if she doesn't stage a protest.

[SEG0057] person_3 (NURSE): Can I flag the HbA1c? There's one from March on the file, but the lab sheet isn't scanned. Just a note that he rang and said the chemist told him it was a bit high, seven-point-something.

[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's the one I was fishing for. Lady at the chemist said seven-point-something, not terrible, keep an eye, and she used the word borderline. I never saw the paper, so it might've been seven-two or seven-eight, I've no idea.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then it's a recalled comment, not a number I can steer by. I'll order a fresh HbA1c today rather than chase a scan that might not exist.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I do that at the usual pathology near work, or does it have to be downstairs?

[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Either place is fine, the form will work at both. My first thought was to lift the Lantus to twenty-four units tonight, to match that old script, and see you again in a month.

[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm walking that back. You're skipping nights, and eighteen versus twenty-four is still unresolved, so putting it up today could drop you on an early shift. We are not changing the insulin dose today.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): That's a relief, I'm not going to pretend otherwise. I came in braced for a lecture and a bigger number on the dial.

[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): No lecture. What I do want is this: keep dialling the eighteen you actually use, including the nights before an early shift, and if you feel hypo you treat it and ring us — you don't just drop the next dose. And bring the pen, the box it came in, and the meter next time.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Eighteen, even on work nights. Alright. I'll park the pen by the kettle so I see it before bed. Alarms don't work on me, I've tried, I just sleep through them.
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): And have a proper look at the feet each night, given the feeling's down on the right. If you find a sore, or it goes red and hot, don't sit on it till the appointment.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum's toe. Yep. I'll look properly, not the quick glance I usually do while the telly's on.

[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm still not going to tell you what's pushing the sugars up. Missed doses are sitting high on the list, the meter units are a muddle, and until that HbA1c is back I won't conclude you're high on our scale, and I won't conclude the dose is wrong either. Let's see what the test says.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): So no new tablet, no extra insulin. Blood test, and come back. That's the whole plan?
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the shape of it. If the HbA1c comes back clearly high, then we might adjust the insulin at that visit — might, not will. I'm not writing a new dose today.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): And the fuzzy newspaper business — do I have to see the eye people again, or is the old letter enough?
[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not if the letter turns up and it's clear. Bring it. If you can't find it, then we'll rebook the retinal photos, but only in that case.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll rummage tonight. My wife knows that drawer better than I do, she'll have it in about thirty seconds, knowing her.
[SEG0074] person_3 (NURSE): I'll put the HbA1c form in the tray. Did you want a urine albumin on the same form, or the kidney bloods, or just the HbA1c?

[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): Just the HbA1c. I was going to add the urine and the kidney tests, but we'll keep it to the one so it actually gets done. We can do the kidneys next round if we need them.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Good call, I hate the pee bottle. Last time I spilled it in the footwell of the car. Long story, you genuinely don't want it.
[SEG0077] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll spare myself. Come back in a fortnight, with the pen, the meter, and the eye letter if it's surfaced. We'll sit with the HbA1c then.
[SEG0078] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. I'll book it out the front on the way past. And I'll try not to skip the pen, even on the early weeks. Mondays are the villain.
[SEG0079] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mondays included. If you have a proper hypo — sweating, shaking, muddled — pull over, have something sweet, and don't keep driving. Ring the clinic the same day.

[SEG0080] person_2 (PATIENT): Got it. There's barley sugar in the glove box already, I'll throw some juice in as well. Thanks for not jumping the dose. I was worried you'd think I was mucking you about with the eighteen and the twenty-four.
[SEG0081] person_1 (DOCTOR): You gave us the messy version, which is the one we can actually use. See you in two weeks.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

bad.reason: Crestor was stopped, but indication 'cholesterol' was not stated by patient.
March HbA1c note existed, but it was not completed/requested by nurse in this transcript.
bad.text: HbA1c (type=laboratory, status=completed, requested_by=nurse, indication=File note from March of a patient call that the chemist said seven-point-something, a bit high and borderline; lab sheet not scanned)

bad.reason: Retinal screen about four months ago is supported; 'requested_by=patient' is not stated.
bad.text: retinal screen (type=imaging, status=completed, requested_by=patient, indication=About 4 months ago at an optometrist; patient recalls a letter saying it was okay and no treatment was needed)

bad.reason: Doctor orders fresh HbA1c due to recalled prior result; unclear meter supports context, but explicit indication omits home meter uncertainty.
bad.text: HbA1c (type=laboratory, status=planned, requested_by=doctor, indication=Fresh result because the previous value is only a recollection and the home meter readings are unclear)

omissions.text: Current insulin use details are incompletely recorded: patient reports Lantus/insulin glargine 18 units at about 9–9:30 pm, but only injects roughly 3–4 nights per week because he skips the dose before 6 am warehouse shifts (Mondays, Tuesdays, sometimes Thursdays).
Patient refused an in-clinic finger-prick glucose; nurse noted no clinic sugar was obtained because he declined it.

Denied shortness of breath was not recorded accurately: patient denied chest pain and tightness, but said he does get puffed on stairs at work and can still talk while doing it, attributing it to being unfit.
Negative eye symptom not captured: patient denied floaters when asked about eyes.
Past medication intolerance detail is incomplete: Crestor (rosuvastatin) was stopped because of muscle aches.
Additional negative findings asked and answered are missing: no foot pain and no redness, and after nail incident patient said it did not break the skin.
Additional history not recorded: patient said a nail injury at work in March was only a fright and did not break the skin.

Management decision detail missing: doctor explicitly considered increasing Lantus to 24 units tonight to match the old script, then reversed that decision and stated insulin dose would not be changed today because 18 vs 24 units is unresolved and skipped doses make an increase potentially unsafe.
Planned investigations were narrowed: doctor decided to order only HbA1c today and defer urine albumin and kidney blood tests until later so the patient would actually get the single test done.

Reason home glucose readings are uncertain is incompletely captured: the home meter was posted from the US years ago, so doctor said the 180-something readings cannot be treated as gospel until the units are known.

The recorded March HbA1c entry is partly wrong: it was not a completed lab result available on file, only a note of a recalled comment ('seven-point-something', 'a bit high', 'borderline') with no scanned lab sheet and no usable numeric result.

clinical_actions.description: Order HbA1c
Rebook retinal photography if the previous eye letter cannot be found
Might adjust the insulin at the next visit if the HbA1c is clearly high; no dose change today
Keep dialling Lantus 18 units every night, including nights before early shifts; treat a hypo and ring rather than skipping the next dose
Bring the insulin pen, its box, and the home meter to the next visit
Check the feet each night, and do not wait for the appointment if a sore appears or the foot becomes red and hot
Bring the retinal-screen letter to the next visit
If a proper hypo occurs, pull over, take something sweet, do not keep driving, and ring the clinic the same day
Follow-up consultation

clinical_uncertainties.description: The patient says he dials Lantus 18 units at night, while the nurse says the chart and script list insulin glargine 24 units at night.
The patient skips Lantus before early shifts, while the nurse notes he had said he takes it every night.
The patient cannot date the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes more precisely than about twelve years ago, around June.
The patient is unsure when the shaky driving episode happened and places it at maybe a year ago.

contradictions_detected: Patient reports dialling Lantus 18 units at night; nurse reports the chart and script say insulin glargine 24 units at night.

Previous HbA1c recalled only as seven-point-something or borderline, with no lab sheet on file

omissions.text: Current Lantus/insulin glargine dose reported by patient is 18 units nightly around 9–9:30 pm; the medication entry lacks the dose.

Patient reports skipping the night-time Lantus on early-shift weeks because of fear of hypoglycaemia while driving, and only injects roughly 3–4 nights per week; this adherence detail is clinically important for interpreting control.

Home glucose readings were specifically fasting values of 176–190 on a US meter with uncertain units; recording this as 'fasting home glucose 180-something' misses that the units may be incompatible and the readings should not be treated as reliable.
Denial of shortness of breath/chest red flag is incomplete: patient denied chest pain and tightness, and said stair puffing is likely deconditioning and he can still talk while doing it.
Negative finding missing: no floaters were reported when asked about eye symptoms.
Negative finding missing: patient denied needing ambulance care / no severe dramatic hypoglycaemic episode.
Allergy history was more specific than 'no allergies': patient stated penicillin had previously been tolerated with no rash or swelling.
Past medication history is incomplete: rosuvastatin/Crestor was stopped because of muscle aches, and the doctor stated it would not be restarted today.
Additional past medical history/trauma detail missing: stood on a nail at work in March, causing no skin break, more of a fright than an injury.
